articles.title: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady in split vote ahead of midterm elections
articles.summary: Federal Reserve officials voted 10-2 to keep interest rates unchanged, as elevated inflation continues to pose a problem for central bankers. Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-point rate hike. The Fed’s benchmark rates remained in the 3.75% to 4% range , as widely expected. A rate hike in December, however, appears far more likely, according to the Fed's dot plot and fed funds futures. Here are the key takeaways from the Fed’s statement and Fed Chairman Warsh’s press conference: Fed upgrades economy from “solid” to “strong”: The FOMC updated the language in its statement, adding that "the accumulation of more information will help" it decide the right policy stance. This suggests the Fed is not in a hurry to ease inflation. But “inflation remains elevated”: Warsh reiterated the Fed’s commitment to bringing inflation down to the 2% target. Although recent inflation data came in hotter than expected , the Fed has positioned itself to continue assessing data. Warsh announces changes to the Fed’s schedule : In 2027, one of the eight Fed meetings will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy with neither a vote on the Fed’s funds rate nor a policy statement. In 2028, policymakers will hold two meetings dedicated to strategy and six for setting policy. Warsh refutes the idea that the decision was politically inflected: Warsh stated that “politics played no role in the decision” — something that generated some discussion with the US midterm elections next week. articles.title: 2 right-wing provocateurs face election-related charges in Minnesota
articles.summary: Two right-wing provocateurs, James O'Keefe and Cam Higby, are facing election-related charges in Minnesota after posting videos of an undercover stunt intended to expose alleged deficiencies in election security . Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said each man faces a count of unlawful voting and identity theft. "Elections are the bedrock of democracy and their protection is one of our highest priorities," Moriarty said in a statement. "Individuals engaging in unlawful conduct related to our elections will be held accountable." Hegseth directs military cyber forces to use 'every authorized asset' to defend midterm elections from foreign interference amid Trump's funding cuts to election security agencies O'Keefe, a self-proclaimed "guerilla journalist" infamous for his undercover videos, and Higby, a social media influencer, posted the video at the heart of the charges in August. It shows the two men approaching election judges at multiple voting precincts in Minneapolis wearing burqas, speaking in fake accents, and allegedly misrepresenting their identities, in an effort to expose what O'Keefe and Higby say are gaps in the rules that allow residents to vouch for the identity of other voters. The video, which remains pinned on Higby's X account, is called "I Wore Burqa To EXPOSE Election FRAUD In Minneapolis." No ballots were cast in the course of their efforts. Tim Evans/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: People fill their ballots during the first day of early voting for the midterm elections in Minneapolis, Minnesota, October 16, 2026. Prosecutors said Wednesday that O'Keefe and Higby deceived the election judges by using the identities of real Minnesota voters "without those voters' knowledge or permission" in violation of state law. Each count carries up to five years in prison and a fine of up to $10,000. Neither man is in custody, according to charging documents. In a statement shared on X, Higby said, "No laws were broken. They want me in PRISON for exposing election vulnerabilities in their state." O'Keefe did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Steve Simon, the state's top election official, said in a statement that "any attempt to disrupt or deceive our election workers will not be tolerated." The charges announced Wednesday in Minnesota are not O'Keefe's first brush with the law. In 2010, O'Keefe pleaded guilty in Louisiana to a misdemeanor charge of entering a federal property under false pretenses after he posed as a telephone repairman to gain access to a U.S. senator's New Orleans office. articles.title: Federal judge who oversaw Trump, Maduro and 9/11 cases dies at 92
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Alvin K. Hellerstein, a Manhattan federal judge who presided over cases involving President Donald Trump , former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and the 9/11 attacks during nearly three decades on the bench, has died. He was 92. Hellerstein died Wednesday morning while surrounded by his family, Chief Judge Laura Taylor Swain said in a statement. His funeral is scheduled for Thursday at Riverside Memorial Chapel in Manhattan. Chief Judge Laura Taylor Swain remembered Hellerstein as a “distinguished jurist” and praised his “energetic and dedicated service” to the court, which continued until his death. “He is greatly appreciated and will be sorely missed,” Swain said. Just two weeks ago, Hellerstein presided over the arraignment of Maduro and Maduro’s wife, Cilia Flores, on torture charges that were added to their ongoing narco-terrorism conspiracy case. Maduro, who was captured alongside his wife in January in a surprise U.S. military raid in Caracas, twice defied Hellerstein’s request that he enter a plea to the charges. Irked, Hellerstein took matters into his own hands, interjecting that “a plea of not guilty will be entered on behalf of Mr. Maduro.” At Flores’ Oct. 8 bail hearing, Hellerstein coughed and struggled to speak at times, telling lawyers: “I have a voice problem. As long as you can understand — hear me, I’ll keep going.” Nevertheless, he was resolute that he’d preside over Maduro and Flores’ trial, which he’d scheduled for next June. Now, another judge will be assigned. “We were saddened to learn of Judge Hellerstein’s passing and offer our condolences to his family,” Maduro's lawyer, Barry Pollack, said. Hellerstein, a New York native and Columbia Law School graduate, served as a first lieutenant in the U.S. Army Judge Advocate General’s Corps and was a Manhattan litigator before President Bill Clinton, a Democrat, appointed him to the federal bench in 1998. He kept a robust docket even after moving to senior status in 2011. In August, in one of his last significant rulings, Hellerstein again spurned Trump’s effort to erase his hush money conviction , rejecting the president’s bid to move the state court case to federal court and have it dismissed on presidential immunity grounds. It was the third time Hellerstein had denied Trump’s requests to move the case. The first time was after Trump’s March 2023 indictment; the second followed Trump’s May 2024 conviction and a subsequent U.S. Supreme Court ruling that presidents and former presidents cannot be prosecuted for official acts. Hellerstein was forced to revisit the matter after the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that he erred in his prior ruling by failing to consider “important issues relevant” to the president’s request . However, the appeals court panel noted that it expressed “no view” on how Hellerstein should rule. In 2020, Hellerstein sprang Trump’s estranged former lawyer and fixer Michael Cohen from prison after the Justice Department revoked his home confinement to thwart his efforts to publish a book or talk to the media. The government’s action, he ruled, was retaliatory and a First Amendment violation. In the aftermath of the 2001 terror attack on the World Trade Center, Hellerstein presided over dozens of wrongful death, injury and property damage lawsuits — a two-decade-long effort that shaped his legacy on the bench. Some of the judge’s former clients died in the attack and, lawyers say, he showed great empathy to victims and their families, meeting with them for hours in his chambers and rejecting what he felt were low-ball settlement offers. In March 2010, Hellerstein rejected as insufficient a settlement that would have paid at least $575 million to thousands of people who fell ill working in the toxic ash of the trade center. He acknowledged he was breaking with tradition by getting so involved in the case. “Most settlements are private. A plaintiff and defendant come together, shake hands, and it’s done with,” he explained. The judge usually has no part in saying yes or no. “This is different,” Hellerstein said. “This is 9/11.” Others were dismayed when, in 2008, Hellerstein ended an effort to force New York City government to keep searching for human remains in debris moved from ground zero to a Staten Island landfill. His other notable recent cases included the criminal trials of Charlie Javice, who was convicted last year of defrauding JPMorgan Chase out of $175 million by exaggerating the customer base for her financial aid startup, and hedge fund founder Bill Hwang, who was convicted in 2024 of securities and market manipulation fraud in a scheme that cost banks billions of dollars. He also presided over a 2025 civil trial at which a jury ordered French bank BNP Paribas to pay nearly $21 million for giving the Sudanese government access to the U.S. financial system as it engaged in atrocities two decades ago. Hellerstein made headlines in 2015, when he ordered a New York City cable company to pay a Texas woman $229,500 for flooding her phone with 153 robocalls. Hellerstein, known for a quirky independent streak and strict discipline in his courtroom, insisted spectators wear pandemic-era masks for years after other judges stopped the practice. Hellerstein “lived a life of commitment to public service and devotion to his community,” the court said in a statement. “His example and work ethic will continue to be a model for this court.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/alvin-k-hellerstein-federal-judge-165439171.html

articles.title: Operatives linked to Mary Peltola's campaign sought GOP spoilers, report shows
articles.summary: Mary Peltola (AP) Operatives working with Democrat Mary Peltola's Senate campaign sought to recruit candidates who could draw votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, according to an investigation published Wednesday. The effort included finding another Alaskan named Dan Sullivan to run against the incumbent, recruiting other potential candidates, and discussing the creation of a conservative political party, The New York Times reports, citing interviews, text messages, and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit. Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee denied recruiting candidates. "The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign and did not recruit any candidates into the race," the campaign said in a statement to the Times. The operation, internally called the ballot composition project, began in summer 2025, according to Elisa Rios, Peltola's former campaign manager. Rios said campaign aides directed a staff member to search voter records for Alaskans named Dan Sullivan. Dan J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher in Petersburg, subsequently entered the race. He has maintained that he decided to run independently and did not respond to the Times' latest requests for comment. The general election ballot includes Peltola, incumbent Dan S. Sullivan, Dan J. Sullivan, and Republican Gerald Heikes. The race could help determine control of the Senate. Sullivan Jr. changed his voter registration from Republican to undeclared, a type of independent, when he requested an absentee ballot for the August primary, according to state election records, reports The Alaska Beacon . He appears on the general election ballot as "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.," without a party label. Incumbent Sen. Sullivan is identified by his party and incumbency. Dan J. Sullivan initially denied requesting the registration change but acknowledged it after election officials provided his application. He maintains that he is running to offer voters an alternative, while President Donald Trump and other Republicans accuse him of trying to undermine the incumbent. The Justice Department has sued to pause certification unless the incumbent wins, arguing that the similar names could confuse voters. Polling shows the incumbent and Democrat Mary Peltola well ahead of Dan J. Sullivan and Republican Gerald Heikes. Rios, who was fired during an August staff shake-up, told the Times that Peltola knew about the project but was not directly involved. "Alaskan voters need to know," Rios said. "There was a lot of speculation, and voters should get the full picture when making their decisions." Rios later sought to retract her statements as the newspaper prepared to publish. She had been considering a wrongful termination lawsuit against the campaign but had not filed one. "As discussed on our call earlier today, I am confirming that I have retracted all statements made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate Race in connection with any article you may or may not be writing," Rios wrote. "I am not willing to be a source for any story in any capacity." The Times said her interviews were on the record and consistent with other reporting. Its investigation included interviews with 12 people and dozens of text messages. Rios identified Democratic operative Jerid Kurtz as a central participant. She said Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee aides introduced him to campaign officials and that he later reported contacting the Sullivan who lives in Petersburg. Kurtz did not respond to the newspaper's requests for comment. Matthew Salisbury, a former House candidate, told the Times that a man identifying himself only as Zane repeatedly encouraged him to run for Senate and offered support through outside spending. Salisbury identified Kurtz from a photograph as the man he met. "I'm not naive," Salisbury said. "I had to have that general idea that they're not in it for me." Salisbury did not enter the race. The Times also reported that Kurtz encouraged Democrat David Leslie to withdraw after Leslie advanced from the August primary. His departure allowed Heikes to take the fourth general election ballot position. Heikes said a man from the Midwest recruited him but did not think the man resembled Kurtz's photograph. The newspaper also obtained messages discussing a proposed MAGA party that could attract conservative candidates. That plan was abandoned in May. Questions about financial support remain disputed. Federal records showed that the pro-Peltola 49th State PAC paid Wingspan Strategies, a firm Kurtz co-owns, about $87,000 this fall, the Times reported. The PAC said it had never hired or paid Kurtz to perform services. Political consultant Jim Lottsfeldt denied Rios' account that he agreed during a dinner with campaign employees to help support long-shot candidates through outside spending. He also denied an association with Alaska Values, a super PAC supporting Heikes, despite his name appearing on advertising paperwork. Alaska's nonpartisan primary system allows candidates to select a party affiliation without party approval, with four candidates advancing to a ranked-choice general election. Republicans unsuccessfully challenged Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy, arguing he was not a good-faith candidate. The Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that neither state law nor the U.S. Constitution provided grounds to remove him. The Justice Department sued last week at President Donald Trump's urging, seeking to block certification if votes for Dan J. Sullivan cost the incumbent victory. Both parties have used tactics to influence Alaska's ballot. In 2024, the state Republican Party supported an effort to keep a Democratic candidate who was incarcerated in New York on the ballot against Peltola. © 2026 Newsmax. articles.title: 4 investigations Democrats could launch if they win control of Congress
articles.summary: Democrats have signalled a willingness to launch probes into both Donald Trump and Pete Hegseth's handling of the Iran war [Getty Images] Democrats in the US Congress are already planning how they would use their power if they win a majority in the House or Senate in next week's midterm elections. Success is by no means guaranteed, even if midterms can sometimes be brutal for the incumbent party that holds the White House. Control of the chamber, however, would give the party power to issue subpoenas - summons to testify or produce documents - as well as additional funding to launch investigations early next year. Democrats are weighing whether to investigate senior figures in the Trump administration - and possibly the president himself. Staffers have begun assembling a list of possible investigations and witnesses, according to people familiar with the discussions. Here are a few potential Democratic targets if the party emerges victorious on 3 November. 1. Trump's family and finances Democrats have made it clear that lucrative deals brokered by the Trump family's vast business empire will be primary targets of any initial investigations. "We want to make sure that [American] taxpayer dollars are being used wisely and not being stolen or pocketed because of corruption," Virginia Democratic Representative Suhas Subramanyam, a member of the House Oversight Committee, told the BBC. Items under consideration for investigation include ties between the administration and corporate entities -  particularly cryptocurrency firms -  as well as the international business dealings of the president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Other topics could include the $400m (£301m) aircraft gifted by Qatar to serve as Air Force One and multimillion-dollar defence contracts awarded to firms linked to the Trump family. "What's shocking to me is not only that this administration, cabinet officials and even the president and his family have been corrupt and self-dealing, but they've been so brazen and open about it," Subramanyam said. The White House has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing. "President Trump is focused on retaining Republican majorities in Congress and doubling down on the progress he has made to lower costs for families," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said. "Democrats have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people, just plans to obstruct and baselessly target President Trump's commonsense agenda," she added. A White House official said the administration is "always prepared" to respond to oversight requests regardless of who is in Congress. [BBC] GUIDE: What are the US midterms? IN DEPTH: The real reasons there are so few young US politicians EXPLORE: Where the US midterms will be won and lost VERIFY: How the US economy is really doing under Trump NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox 2. Hegseth and the Pentagon Democratic lawmakers have vowed to look into Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's handling of the war with Iran that began in February - including the number of civilian casualties, munitions shortfalls, spending and claims of poorly prepared troops and facilities. Other topics, according to a source familiar with the discussions, could include boat strikes in the Caribbean that the administration says are aimed at stopping the flow of drugs into the US. In April, a group of House Democrats filed rare articles of impeachment against Hegseth. They cited the war in Iran and accused him of "high crimes and misdemeanours". Impeachment requires only a simple majority in the House, but conviction - and removal from office - would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate. No cabinet official has ever been removed this way. Some experts believe that the negative publicity that would come from congressional hearings could ultimately lead to Hegseth being fired or resigning from the position. "[If] it looks bad for the White House, and it's a drag on their media attention, President Trump might be likely to cut loose those officials, because he doesn't want that bad press," said David Miller, a political science professor and expert on the presidency at American University in Washington DC. "In a sense that could be a win for the Democrats." Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer under George W Bush, told the BBC that the decision to launch the war should come under scrutiny. "The bigger issue is this: this war was never authorised by the United States Congress, and I don't care who the secretary of defence is," he said. "The constitution says that Congress declares war," he said, and lawmakers should "haul these folks in" to answer questions. In a statement, Pentagon Press Secretary Kingsley Wilson defended Hegseth's record, calling him a "transformative leader" who has "slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters". "By every measurable metric, the Department of War is better under Secretary Hegseth's leadership than before," she said, using the administration's preferred name for the defence department. The aircraft gifted by Qatar to serve as Air Force One is also likely to be the target of Democratic investigations [Getty Images] 3. Immigration and ICE raids Senior Democrats -  including Robert Garcia, the California Democrat tapped to lead the House Oversight Committee should the party take back the chamber - have identified immigration enforcement as a key priority for potential congressional investigations. These could examine allegations of misconduct by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents during immigration raids across the country. But these investigations may prove difficult and politically tricky. In 2024, Trump campaigned on a promise of mass deportations of undocumented migrants - a message that resonated with many of his supporters. But recent polls suggest many Americans, including those who backed Trump in that election, are uncomfortable with some of the tactics used by ICE in American cities so far this year. It means Democrats will have to walk a fine line between opposing ICE tactics and appearing to dismiss broader immigration concerns, Painter told the BBC. 4. A third Trump impeachment Democrats are split on the possibility of attempting to impeach Trump for a third time. Some, such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, have expressed support for an impeachment, citing what they view as an unauthorised war with Iran and other alleged impeachable offences. Others have called for a more cautious approach, arguing that any impeachment is unlikely to end in the Senate voting to remove Trump - who has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing - from office. It is also unclear whether the party could agree on a reason to launch impeachment proceedings. "I can do whatever I want, if I want," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office in October, adding that he sees the impeachment efforts in his first term and the later criminal cases brought against him as "very illegal things". James Comer, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, told the Washington Sun news outlet in June that Democrats were "one-trick ponies" who were "going to go after Trump". There is no guarantee for Democrats that any potential investigation would end with a meaningful outcome. But Subramanyam said their efforts would send a message. "If we do not do something because we are scared of the optics, or we don't think it will be successful, or they stonewall us, that will be bad," he said. "Not just for the next two years, but for the next 20 years." articles.title: Trump floats Ted Cruz for Supreme Court and jokes about why he'd get every vote
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump floated nominating Ted Cruz to the Supreme Court for a future vacancy on the nation's high court, joking that the Texas Republican senator's confirmation would earn unanimous Senate support because senators from both parties would like to see him gone. Trump, who has mentioned Cruz previously for the Supreme Court, suggested the third-term senator again at an Oct. 27 midterm campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas as the president discussed what he might do if he gets to nominate a Supreme Court justice for a fourth time over his two White House terms. "I said, 'I have an answer to not being able to get it past the Democrats or the Republicans together,'" Trump said, referring to the confirmation fight in the Senate. "I would pick Ted Cruz to be the next Supreme Court justice, and I wouldn't have to worry about it. I wouldn't have to make a phone call. "The Democrats will 100% vote for it because they hate the guy and the want to get rid of him," Trump continued. "And the Republicans would 100% vote for it because they can't stand him, they would like to get rid of him. So I'd get 100% of the vote, and he would be a Supreme Court justice and he'd do a great job." More: Trump, Talarico hit different notes in dueling Texas rallies as Senate fight rages Cruz, who was in attendance at the rally for Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, laughed and smiled from his front-row seat as Trump made the pitch. A conservative firebrand in the Senate, Cruz has repeatedly said he's not interested in serving on the Supreme Court. ​“I don't want to be a judge,” Cruz told the Houston Chronicle in September. More: Trump says he regrets nominating Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, Barrett to SCOTUS Trump has openly expressed regret for nominating each of his three Supreme Court picks from his first term ‒ Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett ‒ after they sided against his administration in a series of high-profile rulings. Trump called Cruz "a brilliant guy, brilliant lawyer, brilliant all that." As solicitor general of Texas from 2008 to 2013, Cruz argued multiple cases before the Supreme Court. After graduating from Harvard Law School, Cruz clerked for then-Chief Justice William Rehnquist. Cruz, 55, has turned into one of Trump's strongest allies on the Senate after running against Trump for the Republican nomination for president in 2016. Cruz has also made no secret about his interest in running for president in 2028. Other Trump allies Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are also considered likely contenders to seek the Republican nomination. Were Trump to appoint Cruz to the Supreme Court, however, the field would start to narrow. It is unclear whether Trump will have an opportunity to nominate a fourth justice to the Supreme Court. Justice Samuel Alito in August said he plans to remain on the bench through at least the next session, batting down speculation the conservative justice could step down to allow Trump to choose his replacement. articles.title: Hollywood could get a major lifeline from Congress. California may still lose out.
articles.summary: Credit: Chris Smith/TheWrap In front of the recently refurbished Alex Theatre in Glendale, Calif., flanked by Sen. Adam Schiff and a half-dozen fellow California House Democrats, Rep. Laura Friedman spoke of the urgent need to pass a federal film tax credit to provide a lifeline to hundreds of thousands of film and TV crew members who have struggled as Hollywood production has fled the country. “Sixty-five countries offer incentives we don’t match, and no single state can outbid a foreign government on its own,” the freshman Congresswoman said earlier this month. “Our bipartisan bill is built on labor costs, which means it only pays off when American workers get hired. These are good paying union jobs with benefits and pensions, and I won’t stop fighting until they come home.” Though the politicians at Friedman’s event were all deep blue, the Motion Picture, Television and Entertainment Revitalization Act is far from a partisan bill. With Republicans also lining up to support the bill, there is high optimism on Capitol Hill and among Hollywood lobbyists and producers that Congress will pass the federal incentive during the lame duck session set to begin in early November following the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The highly anticipated bill — which received new life when President Trump endorsed the idea in early September — would provide a much-needed stimulus in American film production, which has been in decline over the last quarter century. If the federal film tax credit passes – and there’s high confidence among lawmakers that it will – industry insiders anticipate that it will trigger a competition between dozens of states to take advantage of an expected surge in production — and that California shouldn’t assume it will get the lion’s share. In a roundtable hosted by TheWrap, film commissioners and soundstage execs who work in California, New Mexico, Georgia and New York said that plans are in motion in their states and others to hit the ground running in 2027 should the bill be signed by Trump. Scott Karol, President/COO of SP Media Group, has had the ear of Trump alongside actor Jon Voight, the administration’s Special Ambassador to Hollywood, and SP Media founder Steven Paul. He told TheWrap he’s been amazed by how quickly both parties, despite the turbulence affecting virtually every other political issue in Washington, have gotten onboard. “People are frustrated that nothing is getting done in politics, but in every discussion I’ve had about the need for a federal tax incentive, the response I’ve gotten has been, ‘This is a good idea. This will help a lot of people. Let’s get it done,’” Karol said. According to a study commissioned by multiple Hollywood unions, the share of production spending committed by major Hollywood studios to film shoots located within the U.S. has decreased from 74% in 1999 to 42% in 2024. The availability of federal tax incentives in countries like the U.K. and Canada on top of local and provincial incentives has been a driving force in that decline, and Karol said that an American equivalent of that has been long overdue. “I’ll tell you what I told President Trump: We don’t need to have the best tax credit. We just need a competitive one,” he said. “The U.S. has the best crews. It has the soundstages and the locations and everything else needed for filming in this country to flourish again. What we need is an incentive structure that eliminates the gap between how expensive it is to film here versus filming elsewhere.” Starting in 2027, that gap may finally be bridged. But while conventional wisdom might suggest that California will be the biggest beneficiary of a federal incentive as Hollywood’s home, it may lose out on much of that anticipated surge to other states that are gearing up with lucrative tax packages and shiny new soundstages to win over studios and indie producers alike. That is, unless it steps up its own incentive game. A four-week blitz There’s a tight window for the federal film credit to get passed when Congress returns to session on Nov. 9. It’s also just one of a long list of items that lawmakers will hope to address before the end of the year. Among those is a government funding bill that must pass before Dec. 11 to avoid another shutdown, a bill to fund farm aid programs that expired at the end of September and an annual vote on the National Defense Authorization Act that has stalled in the Senate over the Trump Administration’s war in Iran. But with bipartisan support and an expected full-scale lobbying push by Hollywood’s studios and unions, confidence is high that the bill can be pushed through both houses and sent to Trump for signature before the targeted Senate adjournment date of Dec. 18. Meanwhile, the pressure is on from the entertainment workforce for the tax credit to deliver as promised. This past week, SAG-AFTRA President Sean Astin cited the actors guild’s lobbying for the bill and other efforts on the state and local levels to boost production as members have become increasingly frustrated over the difficulty of finding employment and reaching the minimum earnings threshold needed to maintain their union healthcare. That annual threshold is set to increase to over $31,000 by 2030, a total that many working actors are falling well short of. “Today, the notion of middle-class life is becoming harder and harder to see. There’s downward pressure on everyone and fewer opportunities all around,” he said. “But what we can do, what your union can do and is doing, is to use every bit of leverage we have to make sure working performers have a place in whatever this industry becomes.” But while the floodgates may be opening for the American film industry, there will be a race between states to collect the productions that pour forth. As several industry insiders told TheWrap, some states may be better positioned to take advantage of the federal credit than others. And as one studio executive noted, the biggest winner of that incentive may not be Hollywood. A competition between states Hollywood’s most scrutinized CEO, Skydance’s David Ellison, is on the same page. Speaking to reporters following the close of Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros., Ellison said that following the settlement of the lawsuit seeking to block that merger he told California Attorney General Rob Bonta that more work needed to be done even with a federal incentive to make California competitive. “Even if you got the federal rebate, California would not be as competitive with some of the other states in the United States,” he said. “Jersey is at 43%. Georgia is at 38%.” While California has raised the annual cap on its state incentive from $330 million to $750 million, producers and studio execs told TheWrap they believe that it’s the tri-state area that’s most likely to see the biggest American production boom in the years ahead. That’s because New York, which has an $800 million cap on its state incentive with a separate $100 million-capped program for indie productions, allows above-the-line spending to be included towards its 30% baseline tax credit — and up to a 40% limit of all other combined qualified costs. New Jersey’s tax credit program is more complicated, with allocations for various types of productions including a $250 million program for studios that sign deals to occupy soundstage complexes in the state like Netflix, Lionsgate and Paramount, the latter of which is set to occupy 1888 Studios, a 1.5 million-square-foot complex being constructed in Bayonne. But as Ellison noted, productions enjoy a 30% base rate that includes above-the-line spending and can reach 44% with bonuses. And then there is Georgia, whose uncapped incentive program and state-of-the-art soundstages like Trilith Studios on the outskirts of Atlanta once made it a mecca for blockbuster filmmaking. But according to state economic data, film and TV output has fallen from a peak of 412 productions with a combined $4.4 billion in direct economic spending in 2022 to 245 productions and $2.3 billion in 2025. Marvel Studios’ “Avengers: Doomsday” was the most high profile move as it was filmed in the U.K. after “Avengers: Endgame” was filmed at Trilith, but it is far from the only one. “The reasons for moving out of the U.S. can vary from studio to studio depending on what soundstage deals they make, but labor costs are the common denominator,” said one production exec at a major studio who spoke on condition of anonymity. “The gap in costs between hiring union in the U.S. and hiring even union in other countries is getting bigger because of that lack of a federal tax credit.” Which is why industry insiders believe that should such an incentive be passed, several U.S. states would immediately take advantage, especially considering that, according to Congressional insiders, the tax credit would be handled by the IRS, eliminating the need to create a federal film commission and allowing the incentive to take immediate effect. But Thomas Laub, producer and EVP of studio strategy for Shadowbox Studios in Georgia, noted how the impacts will be felt state-to-state will depend on several factors, including the aforementioned infrastructure and crew base sizes that Georgia, New York and New Jersey are building. The other key factor, however, is stability. “The U.K. tax credit has been stable for 20 years, whereas I think the fear or the worry, perhaps, of a U.S. federal film incentive is, what if it creates two, three golden years of American production, which would be marvelous, and then in three years — due to political pressure, the desire to cut budget, etc. — that is suddenly perhaps taken away,” Laub said. “How does that affect the states who have used state funding to create some film infrastructure, expended millions and millions of dollars on workforce development to train additional local crews?” Uncapped California? Stability has also been a question for California, where industry lobbyists and lawmakers scrambled to adjust the state’s incentive to account for a new law that puts a cap on tax breaks for all businesses in the state. Independent productions will be exempt from that cap, while major studio productions will be able to take advantage of accelerated payouts. While there had been concerns that the abrupt changes would decrease producers’ confidence in the incentive program and push them towards other states when moving projects back to the U.S. from overseas, studio execs tell TheWrap that the biggest thing holding back California from being truly competitive is the inability to include above-the-line salaries as eligible spending. “The changes they made to what kind of shows can qualify has helped a lot, but as long as that above-the-line rule is there, there’s a big chunk of major productions with large crew sizes that aren’t going to consider California,” said one exec. “And the only way to include above-the-line spending will be to uncap the program, because that’s the only way to satisfy demand, especially with animated features now drawing from that $750 million pool.” Source: FilmLA California is in a paradoxical position. With a labor base that is among the largest in the world thanks to decades as the undisputed center of the entertainment world, the recent decline in Golden State productions has sent thousands of crew members either to other states in search of work or into other careers entirely. But the demand for production incentives that remains is still large enough that unlike other states, California’s program has to establish specific windows during which productions can apply to ensure that incentivized projects shoot in the state year-round, and those that do receive credits must begin shooting within 180 days of approval, which can make some producers who are juggling location availability, actor schedules and other logistical issues reluctant to commit to such a time frame. It is unlikely those rules will change any time soon, as insiders at the California Film Commission say that the 180-day rule is done to ensure that the program fulfills its intended goal as a jobs builder that provides a net boost to the state’s economy. But when California legislators return to Sacramento in 2027, it is expected that there will be a push to uncap the incentive program to avoid getting left behind in the race to capture Hollywood productions moving back to the U.S. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who is running for re-election Nov. 3, has voiced her support for the uncap along with the federal incentive. “Right now, California wouldn’t be in my top 5 states to shoot,” the exec said. “New Jersey, New York, Georgia, Illinois … those are in general the prime spots. Ohio and Kentucky are on the way up too. But California’s still too complicated.” The post Inside the Rush to Secure the Federal Film Tax Credit appeared first on TheWrap . articles.title: Billionaire investor Nelson Peltz makes move to buy struggling Wendy's
articles.summary: Wendy's ( WEN ) may be cooking up burgers for a billionaire soon. Longtime Wendy's investor and former chairman Nelson Peltz of Trian Partners has reportedly offered $1.4 billion to buy the struggling fast food giant , according to an SEC filing. Wendy's shares rose 15% in early trading. The company's market cap was $1.17 billion prior to the deal. A Wendy's spokesperson didn't return a request for comment. A spokesperson for Trian Partners didn't return a request for comment. Billionaire Peltz — while familiar with the operations — would essentially be buying a dumpster fire. After nearly two years of struggles competing with the likes of behemoths McDonald's ( MCD ) and Yum! Brands' ( YUM ) Taco Bell, plus upstarts such as Shake Shack ( SHAK ), Wendy's is on the cusp of a large number of restaurant closures. "With one of its largest franchisees filing bankruptcy in September (although contested by WEN given prior termination of franchise agreement), we think investors likely expect closures to tick higher than expected, but we admit visibility on our side remains somewhat limited and there could still be a range of outcomes," veteran restaurant analyst Andy Barish warned in a recent note. "That said," he added, "given our view that there are likely additional franchise operators in the system facing challenges with leveraged balance sheets, higher interest rates and profitability pressures from higher beef, labor & build costs (like many others in QSR), we think it is prudent to moderate our development estimates and bake in more potential closures over the next 6-12 months, as the company works to strengthen its system." Meritage Hospitality Group, one of Wendy's largest franchise operators, with more than 300 locations, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September following severe margin pressures and an escalating dispute with corporate headquarters. The company reportedly initiated plans to shutter at least 41 locations. Reports emerged this week that it could close up to 60. The high-profile bankruptcy only added grease to the smoldering fire that is the Wendy's restaurant base. Franchisees had already been closing their locations and heading for the hills. Buried inside Wendy's brutal second quarter earnings call was a mention that 289 locations closed in the US during the first half of the year. There are about 5,700 Wendy's in the US, and Barish estimated the Wendy's US store base will be around 5,600 by the end of 2027. The decision on how many more locations will be closed falls on new CEO Bob Wright, who hasn't hidden his view that Wendy's needs to focus on more profitable locations. Wright officially took over as CEO on May 21, adding to the yawning list of executive turnover at the fast food chain over the past two years. He is a seasoned fast food exec who spent the previous five years fixing Potbelly as CEO. Wright's appointment marked a return to Wendy's, where he previously served in several senior leadership roles, including COO. Wright has his work cut out for him in saving Wendy's beyond tightening up the store base count. Wendy's has posted six straight quarters of same-store sales declines, per Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace analysis. Follow Brian Sozzi on X @BrianSozzi , Instagram , and LinkedIn . Tips on stories? Email him at brian.sozzi@yahoofinance.com. articles.title: Trump scraps methane rules days after satellite spots plume near his Texas rally
articles.summary: President Donald Trump on Tuesday pulled back regulations on a major global warming pollutant — just days after a satellite discovered a large plume of methane pouring out of oil and gas wells near the Lubbock, Texas, campaign rally where Trump made his announcement. Governments and the private sector are deploying a wave of new technology to pinpoint methane leaks like never before. But that technological revolution is colliding with political decisions in the U.S. and Europe to weaken regulations that are designed to curb the powerful driver of climate change. “The methane problem,” Trump said Tuesday night. “I'm officially terminating Biden's expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers $45 billion in costs, unlock vast quantities of Texas natural gas and produce 210 million barrels of oil.” American and European regulators alike have argued that the methane rules should be ditched or delayed because they threaten to increase the price and availability of energy, even as new technology identifies gas leaks — and bad actors — with remarkable accuracy. The backtracking could result in more methane emissions as nations around the world are failing to meet their commitments to contain climate change. “You can't reduce what you don't monitor,” said center-left European Parliament lawmaker Thomas Pellerin-Carlin, who opposes steps to delay the bloc’s rules. Methane has 80 times the warming impact of carbon dioxide over a 20-year period. Climate scientists say controlling methane, a byproduct of producing oil, gas and coal, along with agriculture and decomposing waste, is the fastest way to arrest rising temperatures. But the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has proposed weakening methane standards for oil and gas operators and is poised to eliminate penalties for so-called “super-emitters.” Meanwhile, the European Union is preparing to delay methane rules designed to prioritize energy imports with lower emissions. The backsliding comes as a wave of new technologies has pinpointed the world’s largest sources of methane, making it easier than ever before to prevent the gas from escaping into the atmosphere. A sweeping study published in the journal Nature found that methane-sensing equipment on satellites detected leaks with 92% to 100% accuracy on clear days, underscoring leaps in progress. Satellites are not the only improvement. Heat cameras can now spot leaks. Companies like Google are using artificial intelligence tools to map plumes from space. And firms are flying airplanes with a remote sensing technology that uses laser pulses, called LIDAR, to track methane. “Ten years ago, the tools were not there. You couldn’t detect these things,” said Riley Duren, CEO of the environmental nonprofit Carbon Mapper, which uses satellites and other technologies to detect methane leaks worldwide. “Today we have more tools at our disposal than ever. It’s not a visibility challenge anymore.” The group’s Tanager-1 satellite spotted methane leaks in a slice of the Texas Permian Basin on Oct. 10. Two days later, a new satellite named Tanager-2, which rode a SpaceX rocket into orbit this month, confirmed the Texas plume. The bigger test is getting companies to take action. Carbon Mapper this year has issued 460 notices to companies operating super-emitting sites in 13 U.S. states. It also works with California’s environmental regulator, the California Air Resources Board, on the only U.S. methane enforcement regime that uses satellite technology. Only about half of the recipients responded, Duren said. When asked why, he said states have differing levels of incentives — or punishments — to fix leaks. Many lack personnel. The absence of national policy doesn’t help. The story is similar across the world. The United Nations Environment Programme’s Methane Alert and Response System, which issues alerts from 35 satellites to 24 nations and nine subnational governments, registered a 12% response rate in 2025. The 141 governments that crafted methane reduction goals as part of the Paris climate agreement have done little to meet their targets: Just 20 countries have outlined steps to slash fossil fuel methane emissions, and only five have submitted quantified targets. “It’s clear that there’s a gap between what is being committed and what is being implemented,” said Marcelo Mena-Carrasco, the executive director of the Global Methane Hub, a philanthropy-backed organization working to reduce emissions. “We know this in a much better way — we know who and which companies are doing so, and so we have all the elements to maintain accountability.” Except for enforcement regulations. Shifting geopolitics and a growing focus on securing energy supplies have pushed climate action down many countries’ priority lists. Industry has argued that many methane policies were ill-designed, and there has been pushback to what some companies viewed as a naming and shaming approach when emissions around their operations were identified, said Antoine Halff, who co-founded Kayrros, a firm that tracks methane emissions . The American Petroleum Institute, which represents U.S. oil and gas producers, praised Trump’s proposed rollback of the Biden-era methane limits. “We look forward to working with the Trump administration on a more workable approach that supports American energy production, provides greater regulatory certainty and advances continued emissions reductions,” Dustin Meyer, the group’s senior vice president of policy, economics and regulatory affairs, wrote in a statement. The current energy crisis resulting from the war in Iran has made governments anxious about taking any measures that could push up prices or curtail supply. Even though experts and the European Commission have said that the bloc’s incoming methane rules pose no risks to affordability or energy security, the fossil fuel industry, with the backing of the Trump administration , has seized on these worries to campaign for a delay — successfully. The Commission earlier this month proposed a one-year delay to rules meant to ensure oil and gas companies monitor and report their emissions. The requirement was supposed to inform a subsequent move toward curbing imports from the most polluting gas fields. The Commission also allowed countries to suspend penalties under the regulation. Then last week the European Parliament voted for a three-year postponement of the rules, and some EU governments are pushing for national capitals to adopt a similar delay, citing the energy crisis. Proponents of regulation have pointed out that by patching leaks, companies retain more gas to sell on the market. "We have independent scientific studies that show there is enough regulation-compliant gas on the market to supply the EU twice over. That means giving in to the lobbying right now is just a gift to the fossil fuel industry,” said German Green lawmaker Jutta Paulus. “After all, the gas that escapes unused is precisely what won’t end up on the market. In other words, we’re actually making the supply even scarcer rather than increasing it.” Smaller gas producers have long argued that measures to curb methane are costly. In the current environment, even bigger players who put in place measures to address their methane footprint are less interested in pushing forward. “The impetus toward certification of good methane and responsible gas and so on seems to be fading a bit,” said Halff. “I think this has to do with the extreme uncertainty in the market and concerns about energy security. … I think people are very comfortable pushing this discussion in the background to keep their options open in the future.” Methane measures haven’t completely halted. “There are definitely rollbacks in the U.S. In the EU, I would call it more of a delay than a rollback, but politically it is not the momentum that we would like to see. But I do think that in many other countries … we do have more positive success stories,” said Brandon Locke, director for global methane policy at the Clean Air Task Force, a nonprofit. China, the world’s largest methane producer, has included methane emissions in its latest national climate plan and created standards, rules and measuring and verification systems to curb coal mine methane, its biggest source of emissions . Japan and South Korea established a transparency initiative that asks liquefied natural gas suppliers to disclose their efforts to monitor and address methane leaks — though it’s based on self-reporting. And Kazakhstan, one of the world’s super-emitters due to its aging Soviet-era equipment, has dramatically reduced its methane emissions and is creating national rules to monitor them. That program is based on the EPA super-emitter program, which was enabled by advancements that allowed satellites to track performance across wider basins, said Duren, of Carbon Mapper. Canada’s enhanced methane regulations , which will take effect in 2028, prohibit flaring, put strict limits on venting and call for regular leak detection and repair. But they also allow oil and gas producers to determine how they’ll reduce their emissions, as long as they meet certain standards. The rules are weaker than those that were proposed during the Trudeau administration. “Where there has been sustained long-term efforts by governments to work with industry to systematically reduce emissions, there has been significant reductions and there's lower emissions,” said Stephane Germain, president of GHGSat Inc., which operates 20 satellites that continuously monitor and orbit the Earth. “I'll point to my own backyard here — British Columbia [and] Alberta — two jurisdictions where we rarely see anything with our satellites.” Those measures are all occurring at a time when energy demands are growing rapidly, and countries are using more coal and drilling for more oil to meet them. The U.N.’s latest assessment of the gap between what countries have committed to do on climate and what their policies will actually deliver shows that methane emissions haven’t fallen in the five years since countries pledged to drive them down 30% by 2030. That pledge, launched by the U.S. and EU, put methane on the map globally and mobilized billions of dollars in investment and a major new push on policy, including in China, said Rick Duke, a former deputy climate envoy at the State Department during the Biden administration. But the results of all that attention and money have been underwhelming, said Paulus, the German member of the European Parliament who negotiated the methane law. “We don’t need a Global Methane Pledge if no one's willing to do anything,” she said. articles.title: Hasan Piker sues CNN's Scott Jennings for defamation
articles.summary: Progressive Twitch streamer Hasan Piker filed a defamation lawsuit against conservative CNN commentator Scott Jennings on Tuesday, accusing him of falsely claiming Piker advocated for lynching Black Americans after airing an edited video of his remarks. The 38-page lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., centers on an Aug. 11 episode of “The Scott Jennings Show,” in which Jennings shared clips of Piker claiming he had said, “the USA should resume lynchings against Black people.” Piker, who threatened legal action in August over the claim and shared further context to the clips, alleges Jennings knowingly misrepresented sarcastic comments he made during his livestreams by turning it into an apparent endorsement of racial violence. “Mr. Jennings did not merely mischaracterize something Mr. Piker said,” the complaint reads. “He took a false, fabricated, and manipulated video of Mr. Piker, added a made-up quotation that Mr. Piker never uttered, and then made accusations that went beyond even what the manipulated footage purported to show.” During the August broadcast, Jennings warned Black voters to pay close attention before playing the clip, which included an on-screen caption attributing a statement, “Let’s go back to a better time when lynchings were happening,” to Piker. Jennings later accused Piker of “calling for Black voters to be lynched” and referred to what he called “the Piker plan of returning our country to lynchings.” The original footage came from an October 2024 Twitch broadcast in which Piker was reacting to a debate between two Black political commentators — one liberal and one conservative. After the conservative participant criticized “woke DAs,” Piker sarcastically suggested the commentator wanted to return to an era of racial discrimination and lynchings, according to the complaint. “He said, ‘We need more Klansmen, OK? Can we go back to a better time when lynchings were happening?’” Piker said during the stream in reaction to the commentator’s argument. Piker’s attorneys argue that the edited video removed the words “He said,” along with his laughter and surrounding commentary, to intentionally make it appear as though Piker was expressing his own beliefs rather than mocking someone else’s. The dispute emerged amid the Michigan Senate race , where the edited video was circulated to criticize progressive Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed over his association with Piker. When Jennings posted the segment on the social platform X, he referred to Piker as El-Sayed’s “best pal and campaign partner,” before accusing him of supporting racial violence. The post has received roughly 2.5 million views as of Tuesday, according to the lawsuit, and Jennings allegedly refused to retract his statements despite receiving a written demand from Piker’s attorneys on Aug. 31. Piker’s legal team also says the accusations damaged his reputation and threatened his ability to earn money through streaming, advertising and sponsorships. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. articles.title: 48万票左右以色列大选最终格局？特殊选票初估低于预期，内塔尼亚胡组阁仍缺多数
articles.summary: 以色列议会选举的权力争夺进入关键阶段。以色列中央选举委员会预计，仍有多达48万张“双层信封”特殊选票待清点，数量低于此前最高65万张的准备规模。这批选票理论上可能影响约12个议席，而内塔尼亚胡领导的右翼阵营与反对派目前均未获得议会多数，最终计票结果将影响各方的组阁筹码。 据央视新闻当地时间10月28日，以色列中央选举委员会表示，本次议会选举的特殊选票数量初步估计为43万至48万张，低于此前媒体报道的约60万张。此类选票主要来自以军士兵、服刑人员、驻外外交人员，以及其他无法前往指定投票站的选民。 央视指出，在以色列政坛，平均每4万张票决定议会1个席位，因此这批最后清点的“特殊选票”往往会成为决定各党派席位乃至影响组阁的关键变量。 不过，特殊选票的数量并不等于最终可能发生变化的席位数，实际影响仍取决于各党获得的有效选票及最终议席分配。 初估特殊选票上限较预估最高准备相差17万票，约12个议席仍存变数 以色列中央选举委员会最新估计显示，本次大选的“双层信封”特殊选票预计为43万至48万张，明显低于该委员会此前所做的准备——即预估可能出现多达65万张此类选票。 据《以色列时报》报道，这类选票尚待单独清点，选举官员需要先核实选民身份，并确认其没有在其他地点重复投票，之后才能计入正式结果。由于审核程序复杂，特殊选票通常晚于普通选票完成统计。 这类选票主要来自军人、服刑人员、驻外外交人员等无法在指定投票站投票的选民。上述报道称，以色列中央选举委员会此前之所以做出较高预估，是考虑到以色列在战争期间大规模动员预备役人员，同时部分居民因战事离开原居住地。换言之，特殊选票的规模受到选民投票地点变化的影响。 按照每约4万张选票对应一个议席的粗略估算，43万至48万张特殊选票涉及约12个议席。不过，这只是衡量潜在影响的估算，并不意味着最终会有12个议席发生变化。 以色列采用比例代表制，政党能否跨过3.25%的选举门槛，以及各党最终获得多少有效选票，都会影响席位分配。对于接近门槛的小党而言，特殊选票甚至可能决定其能否进入议会，并间接改变其他政党的议席数量。 因此，尽管特殊选票初估规模低于此前预期，其最终分布仍可能影响各阵营的席位差距与组阁谈判。 初步计票显示双方均未过半，右翼阵营暂时领先 截至10月28日，以色列中央选举委员会公布的部分计票结果显示，内塔尼亚胡领导的右翼阵营暂时领先，但距离组建多数政府仍有差距。 在超过85%的选票完成统计后，部分结果显示，内塔尼亚胡阵营预计获得53席，前以色列国防军总参谋长加迪·艾森科特领导的反对派阵营预计获得48席，阿拉伯政党合计约19席。 以色列议会共有120席，组建获得议会多数支持的政府通常需要至少61席。按照上述初步席位分布，内塔尼亚胡阵营仍缺8席，艾森科特领导的反对派阵营也无法单独组阁。 与最初的出口民调相比，实际计票中的部分结果一度对内塔尼亚胡更为有利。但随着剩余选票继续统计，席位分布仍可能发生变化。 路透社10月28日报道称，内塔尼亚胡与艾森科特均宣称自己有机会领导下一届政府，但两人都没有明确的组阁多数。选举结果反映出以色列政治格局依然分裂，后续政府组成可能需要经历较长时间的谈判。 这也意味着，当前的席位领先并不等于已经获得执政权。最终结果不仅取决于特殊选票，还取决于小党能否跨过选举门槛，以及各党在正式结果公布后如何选择政治联盟。 阿拉伯政党议席增加，反对派组阁仍面临现实障碍 阿拉伯政党在本次选举中的表现，是影响最终组阁格局的另一项关键因素。 随着计票推进，阿拉伯政党获得的议席一度升至19席。它们总体上反对内塔尼亚胡继续执政，因此在议会席位算术上，可能成为反对派争取支持时的重要力量。 但阿拉伯政党的议席并不能直接转化为反对派的组阁优势。以色列不同政党在巴勒斯坦问题、国家安全政策及国内治理等方面存在明显分歧，能否形成稳定的合作关系仍是未知数。 艾森科特及其领导的反对派阵营面临的现实问题是，即使在议席总数上形成优势，也必须争取其他政治力量支持，才能达到61席的多数门槛。 内塔尼亚胡则倾向于组建右翼政府，并排斥依赖阿拉伯政党支持的执政安排。这意味着，阿拉伯政党即使拥有较大的议席规模，也未必能够轻易帮助反对派建立稳定政府。 在这种情况下，特殊选票的分布可能改变各党之间的谈判筹码，但最终组阁结果仍取决于政治立场与联盟谈判，而非单纯的席位加总。 正式结果公布前，组阁谈判仍存多种可能 以色列大选的最终结果仍需等待计票完成。特殊选票的身份核验与统计程序，以及部分政党能否跨过选举门槛，都可能影响最终议席分布。 按照以色列的组阁程序，正式选举结果公布后，总统艾萨克·赫尔佐格将与各政党代表磋商，并指定其认为最有可能组建新政府的候选人。获指定者需要在规定期限内争取足够的议会支持。 如果内塔尼亚胡阵营最终仍无法获得多数，其可能需要争取其他政党加入，或探索更广泛的联合执政安排。艾森科特领导的反对派也面临同样的挑战：如何协调不同政党的政策分歧，并形成能够实际执政的联盟。 如果双方均无法成功组阁，以色列可能再次面临提前举行选举的局面。在新政府成立之前，现任内阁将继续以看守政府身份履职。 对内塔尼亚胡而言，当前的关键是能否将初步计票中的领先转化为足够的议会支持；对反对派而言，则是如何把选举表现转化为真正的执政优势。 特殊选票初估规模低于此前预期，并未消除以色列大选的悬念。随着最终计票推进，真正决定政治走向的仍是各阵营能否争取到61席，以及各党能否跨越政治分歧，组建获得议会支持的新政府。 风险提示及免责条款 articles.summary: 沙特阿拉伯正通过红海与霍尔木兹海峡双线并行的出口格局，打破外界对波斯湾原油供应中断的悲观预期，令中东实货市场的溢价在短短一个月内大幅收窄。 船舶追踪机构初步数据显示，沙特10月迄今的原油日出口量维持在接近战时高位的水平，整体表现与9月相当。与此同时，波斯湾地区其他主要产油国的出口也在向冲突前水平回归，供应紧张的预期正在松动。 供应回暖已直接传导至实货价格。衡量海湾地区现货市场强弱的阿曼-迪拜原油价差，本月早些时候跌至7月以来最低，本周二已降至约6美元/桶，而9月这一数字接近34美元/桶，单月降幅逾80%。 东西管道恢复，双通道打通供应瓶颈 沙特出口韧性的核心，在于东西输油管道的复通。该管道此前因袭击被迫停运，沙特出口一度完全依赖经霍尔木兹海峡的东海岸航线。 管道恢复运营后，沙特重新激活了红海沿岸的延布港出口通道，使其得以同时运用两条出口路线，在应对也门胡塞武装持续袭扰的同时，维持高位出货。 根据数据提供商Vortexa的数据，沙特10月迄今经红海方向（主要为延布港）的日出口量达250万桶，高于9月的240万桶；经波斯湾方向的日出口量为400万桶，较9月的420万桶略有回落，原因是该航线仍受到间歇性袭击干扰。 综合两线，Vortexa统计的沙特10月日均出口量约为650万桶，与9月的660万桶基本持平。 不过，不同机构的数据存在明显分歧。Tankertrackers.com估计10月迄今日出口量约为699万桶，接近冲突前水平；Kpler则估算仅为540万桶，低于9月。 数据差异的主要原因在于，大量油轮已开始关闭卫星应答器以规避袭击风险，导致追踪难度上升。这一信息盲区也给交易员和投资者评估区域供应形势带来了挑战。 买家重返延布港，欧洲现货补量同步推进 出口通道打通的同时，沙特国家石油公司沙特阿美正积极恢复延布港的买家客源。 据彭博援引知情人士透露，阿美已要求部分亚洲买家从11月起重新从延布港提货，此前这些买家中断延布港提货已长达三个月，转而通过穿梭油轮和管道联络经埃及地中海港口取油，以规避红海的胡塞威胁。 在欧洲市场，据彭博此前报道，阿美亦已通知此前遭取消合同的欧洲买家，可就本月及下月的货物参与现货竞购，以弥补此前的缺量。 与此同时， 沙特已向石油输出国组织（OPEC）报告，9月产量提升了三分之一，达到超过830万桶/日的战时高位。 沙特国内炼厂通常每日消耗约300万桶，但亚赞炼油厂（日处理能力40万桶）因胡塞袭击目前仍处于停工状态。 波斯湾整体供应趋向修复 沙特之外，波斯湾地区其他主要产油国的出口形势也在趋于正常化。 科威特完全依赖霍尔木兹海峡出口，其油企高层已表示出口已恢复至冲突前水平；伊拉克上月出口量亦接近战前水平；阿联酋在油轮过境霍尔木兹海峡方面表现最为成功，据国际能源署数据，其产量已升至历史高位。 多路供应同步改善，共同压低了中东实货市场的风险溢价。 阿曼-迪拜价差从9月的近34美元/桶骤降至本周的约6美元/桶，表明此前市场对波斯湾供应的担忧已在相当程度上得到缓解。 然而，地区局势并未彻底平稳。胡塞武装对沙特机场及油气设施的袭击仍在持续，近期攻击已实际影响到利雅得金融区的正常运转，并对沙特整体经济产生外溢压力。油轮信息透明度的下降，也使市场对真实供应量的研判持续存在不确定性。 对沙特而言，在战时维持高油价收益的同时守住出口规模，仍是一道需要持续应对的双重考验。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。
